item.title: C Random Number Generation: Techniques and Best Practices
item.description:
“C Random Number Generation: Techniques and Best Practices”

Generating random numbers in C involves several approaches, ranging from simple pseudo-random number generators (PRNGs) to more robust and cryptographically secure methods. The choice depends heavily on your application’s requirements for randomness quality and security.

Here are various techniques and code examples for generating random numbers in C:

Using rand() and srand()

The most basic approach involves the rand() function from <stdlib.h>, which returns a pseudo-random integer between 0 and RAND_MAX. To ensure different sequences of random numbers on each program execution, you must seed the generator using srand().

item.title: C++ Generating Uniform Random Integers in a Range: Methods Compared
item.description:
“C++ Generating Uniform Random Integers in a Range: Methods Compared”

How does one reliably generate a pseudo-random integer that falls uniformly within a specified inclusive range, say [min, max], in modern or legacy C++? The core challenge is avoiding the statistical bias introduced by simple modulo operations (%) on the output of basic random functions like rand().

Several approaches exist, ranging from the antiquated yet simple to the statistically robust and contemporary.

item.title: C Language rand() Generates Same Sequence: How to Fix with srand()
item.description:
“C Language rand() Generates Same Sequence: How to Fix with srand()”

Many developers encounter a common issue when using the rand() function in C: it consistently generates the same sequence of numbers across different program executions. This behavior can be perplexing, especially when true randomness is expected. The core reason behind this predictability lies in the nature of pseudo-random number generators (PRNGs) and the concept of a “seed.”

At its heart, rand() employs an algorithm to create numbers that appear random but are, in fact, deterministic. The sequence of these numbers is determined by an initial value known as the seed. If this seed remains constant, the PRNG will always follow the same path, producing the same output.
